sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: This independent MLX implementation preserves exact CPU training/per-level inference equivalence and demonstrates coarse-to-fine generation on a finite synthetic language and Sudoku. The funded small-generator recipe reports 97.25–98.10% easy, 79.60–83.40% medium and 33.25–40.30% hard solving across two seeds at equal exposure. We regard this as partial implementation and small-model success, with substantial failures on hard boards and unresolved provenance and reproducibility limits. It does not reproduce Original NCM’s scores or establish matched-cost superiority. The observed seed difference warrants better diagnostics rather than attributing the deficit to a single component. An inference-only port runs the released checkpoints of Kumbong et al. and agrees with upstream PyTorch in the tested computations, up to stated precision effects. Small TinyStories models trained here reconstruct held-out windows accurately but generate text that an external scorer rates far worse than a similarly built autoregressive baseline (generative perplexity 45.568–97.776 against 14.311–14.676). Across two generator seeds on one frozen codec, reducing conditioning corruption lowered clean teacher-forced code loss and worsened free-running text. These text results come from synthetic prose, unconditional generation and unmatched total compute, and they establish no conditional capability. Follow-up runs with the same frozen codec show that the quality gap falls as the generator grows and sees more data: the ratio of NCM to AR generative perplexity goes from 3.33 (11.8M parameters) to 2.38 (87.4M) at the original data and to 2.13 with four times the data, while corruption and loss-weighting variants and sampling policies do not lower it materially (stronger corruption raises it), and bf16 training matches fp32 at 11.8M. These runs are single-seed except one, unmatched in compute and mixed in precision, and the step from 49.6M to 87.4M is smaller than the seed-to-seed difference measured at 11.8M, so they describe a trend, not a scaling law. The XSum generator released by Kumbong et al. also runs in the port and reproduces its published unguided ROUGE scores to within 0.1 and, at guidance weight 0.5, the guided ones to within 0.2. The unresolved gaps are the hard-Sudoku deficit, the autoregressive quality gap on text (still above two at the largest size), the single-codec dependence and the absence of human ratings and of well-trained models on naturally occurring text.

sec.title: Code and reproducibility
sec.p: Code, configurations and this paper: github.com/janmus1c/ncm-mlx. Every configuration is in configs/; measured runs are logged in docs/EXPERIMENTS.md. The benchmark guide explains budget matching, parameter accounting, synchronization and uncertainty. The TinyStories training and evaluation source that produced Section 10 is identified by per-file SHA-256 digests in docs/research/e21-e23-evidence.json, together with configuration, data, tokenizer and scorer identities, checkpoint hashes and per-seed scores. The development commit named there is not in the public history; 41 of its 44 digested training files are byte-identical in the public repository, and the other three, in the released-checkpoint port, also contain later prefix-cache, compilation and benchmark changes. The 44 digested training files, exactly as they were run, are attached to the paper release as the archive ncm-mlx-text-training-source-d323f4f.tar.gz (SHA-256 7c5f9d6e08f70eda075a4d35556bd46a3ef4cc622756f36545915040879a0c64) (download); the digest of each file inside it matches the evidence extract. The aligned evaluation and benchmark driver is not part of the repository or the archive. A clean checkout does not yet reproduce those runs end to end, and the released package ncm-mlx 0.2.0 did not include the text-training commands (they ship from 0.3.0); the commands below cover the Sudoku path. The Section 11 configurations are configs/tinystories-ladder-*.json, tinystories-e21-bf16.json, tinystories-matched-constant.json, tinystories-stronger-corruption*.json and tinystories-equal-level-loss*.json (output directories under artifacts/), and their evaluation numbers are in docs/research/tinystories-scaling.json. These runs used the repository’s text-training workflow with its optional bf16 mixed precision (train.precision). The stronger-corruption and equal-level-loss runs additionally used gradient accumulation of 2 × 32 on a 12 GB card. Accumulation is an option of the unreleased source that ran them; the public code and configurations have no such option and train the same recipe as one batch of 64, which needs more memory and is not bitwise the same computation. The sampling-policy study (Section 11.2) is run by scripts/sampling_study.py with the 98-run list scripts/sampling_study_runs.json. It is the private script that produced the tables, cleaned up for release, and it has not been re-run on a clean checkout. The FineWeb-Edu data preparation is private and not in the repository, so Section 11.5 cannot be reproduced from it. The audited reports, sample outputs and scorer records for Section 11 are attached to the paper release as the archive ncm-mlx-tinystories-evidence-e25-e32.tar.gz (SHA-256 cbe6ec001b53a6f09a2b2b8fed4fce711852379cb42f6c277129b851bdfe430d, download); the numbers in docs/research/tinystories-scaling.json were read from its report.json files. Scorer records exist for E25 and E28 only; the other runs keep their per-seed perplexities in the reports. The archive holds no model weights. The XSum port runs as python -m ncm_mlx official summarize --task xsum, and scripts/official_xsum_parity.py reproduces the parity check against upstream PyTorch. Audited reports, sample outputs and per-output scorer records for all six runs are attached to the paper release as ncm-mlx-tinystories-evidence-e21-e24.tar.gz (SHA-256 4a744f5306ebef3433abbab9647372d6ad00949f616c7befe9476fbccb0d20b8, download).

sec.p: Later Sudoku runs reuse the frozen E6 codec and its 12-level, 16-code hierarchy. All use an 81-cell prefix, eight attention heads, configured generator seed 0 except E20 (seed 1), AdamW with weight decay 0.01, a cosine learning-rate schedule and compiled generator training. Generator dropout is 0.1 at width 256 and 0.2 at width 512; warmup is 200 steps at width 256 except E19/E20, which use 1,000; width 512 also uses 1,000. The codec is additional to the generator sizes below.

caption.p: Later Sudoku generator settings. Steps are completed steps for the reported results; corruption gives the first and last replacement probabilities.

sec.p: The base data are 200,000 training puzzles and 1,000 validation puzzles, with split seed 0 and 28–45 givens. E15 adds one million greedy-unique puzzles for each seed 201–204; E16 adds one million for each seed 205–206. E17 adds the unique subset of one million random-removal candidates for each seed 101–104; its final 2,000 steps are a weights-only continuation with reset optimizer and random state (Section 6.5). E12’s recorded run completed 50,776 steps; the repository’s current E12 configuration specifies 200,000, so running that configuration unchanged does not reproduce the reported exposure. E18 adds no unique-puzzle corpus. Both E19 runs and E20 add one million greedy-unique puzzles per seed 201–208; their separate schedules use full-state snapshots every 1,000 updates. The original million-step E19 configuration remains unstarted and is not either reported result. Full settings and checkpoint prerequisites are in the corresponding configs/sudoku-e*.json files and docs/EXPERIMENTS.md.

TinyStories settings (Section 10). Codec: 12 levels of lengths 1, 8, 16, 24, 32, 40, 52, 64, 76, 92, 108, 128 with 2,048 codes each, width 256, 4 heads, 14,000 updates at batch 256, learning rate 5e-4 with cosine decay to 5e-5, warmup 1,000, weight decay 0.01, dropout 0.3, fine-level dropout 0.5, commitment 0.25, EMA decay 0.95. Generator: 6 × 384, 6 heads, dropout 0.1, 15,000 updates at batch 64, warmup 500, weight decay 0.1, betas (0.9, 0.95), gradient clipping 1, loss \alpha = 0 α=0. AR baseline: same stack, 7,500 updates at batch 128. Corruption endpoints: 0.75 → 0.25 (E21, E24), 0.30 → 0.05 (E22) and 0 → 0 (E23); E24 and the seed-1 repeats of E22 and E23 differ only in configured seed 1 and reuse the seed-0 codec.

Section 11 settings. All runs: the TinyStories codec and settings above, with the frozen E21 codec reused. Generators: 6 × 384 × 6 heads (11,832,587 parameters), 12 × 576 × 9 heads (49,644,683) and 12 × 768 × 12 heads (87,426,059); the AR baseline of each size uses the same blocks (13,794,048, 52,586,880 and 91,348,992 parameters). Data multiple 1×: generator 15,000 updates at batch 64, AR 7,500 at batch 128, fp32. Data multiple 4×: generator 60,000 updates at batch 64 (3,840,000 windows), AR 30,000 at batch 128, train.precision = "bfloat16". The bf16 parity run is the E21 recipe with train.precision = "bfloat16". Corruption variants: matched constant 0.3878 (E25); 0.90 → 0.50 (E28); equal level loss \alpha = 1 α=1 with the E21 corruption (E28). The FineWeb pipeline check (E26) uses 14 × 768 × 12 heads and 20 × 1024 × 16 heads generators, batch 16 and 8, peak learning rate 3e-4, corruption 0.75 → 0.25, on 800,000 training windows of 128 tokens.
